claim: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium is a facultative intracellular pathogen that utilizes its type III secretion systems (T3SSs) to inject virulence factors into host cells and colonize the host.
source: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium is a facultative intracellular pathogen that utilizes its type III secretion systems (T3SSs) to inject virulence factors into host cells and colonize the host.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field supported by the manuscript's introduction and citations to prior work.

claim: A subset of cytosolic immune receptors respond to T3SS ligands by forming multimeric signaling complexes called inflammasomes.
source: In turn, a subset of cytosolic immune receptors respond to T3SS ligands by forming multimeric signaling complexes called inflammasomes, which activate caspases that induce interleukin-1 (IL-1) family cytokine release and an inflammatory form of cell death called pyroptosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of innate immunity and inflammasome biology.

claim: Inflammasomes activate caspases that induce interleukin-1 (IL-1) family cytokine release and pyroptosis.
source: In turn, a subset of cytosolic immune receptors respond to T3SS ligands by forming multimeric signaling complexes called inflammasomes, which activate caspases that induce interleukin-1 (IL-1) family cytokine release and an inflammatory form of cell death called pyroptosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about inflammasome function.

claim: Human macrophages mount a multifaceted inflammasome response to Salmonella infection that ultimately restricts intracellular bacterial replication.
source: Human macrophages mount a multifaceted inflammasome response to Salmonella infection that ultimately restricts intracellular bacterial replication.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Caspase-1 is essential for mediating inflammasome responses to Salmonella in human macrophages.
source: We find that caspase-1 is essential for mediating inflammasome responses to Salmonella and restricting bacterial replication within human macrophages, with caspase-4 contributing as well.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing loss of inflammasome responses in CASP1-/- cells.

claim: Caspase-1 is essential for restricting bacterial replication within human macrophages.
source: We find that caspase-1 is essential for mediating inflammasome responses to Salmonella and restricting bacterial replication within human macrophages, with caspase-4 contributing as well.
evidence: This is supported by CFU data and microscopy showing increased bacterial burdens in CASP1-/- cells.

claim: Caspase-4 contributes to restricting bacterial replication within human macrophages.
source: We find that caspase-1 is essential for mediating inflammasome responses to Salmonella and restricting bacterial replication within human macrophages, with caspase-4 contributing as well.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased bacterial burdens in CASP4-/- cells at later timepoints.

claim: Gasdermin D (GSDMD) plays a role in controlling Salmonella replication in human macrophages.
source: We also demonstrate that the downstream pore-forming protein gasdermin D (GSDMD) and Ninjurin-1 (NINJ1), a mediator of terminal cell lysis, play a role in controlling Salmonella replication in human macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased bacterial burdens in GSDMD-/- cells and with disulfiram treatment.

claim: Ninjurin-1 (NINJ1) plays a role in controlling Salmonella replication in human macrophages.
source: We also demonstrate that the downstream pore-forming protein gasdermin D (GSDMD) and Ninjurin-1 (NINJ1), a mediator of terminal cell lysis, play a role in controlling Salmonella replication in human macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased bacterial burdens with NINJ1 knockdown and glycine treatment.

claim: In the absence of inflammasome responses, Salmonella hyperreplicates within the cytosol of infected cells.
source: Notably, in the absence of inflammasome responses, we observed hyperreplication of Salmonella within the cytosol of infected cells as well as increased bacterial replication within vacuoles, suggesting that inflammasomes control Salmonella replication primarily within the cytosol and also within vacuoles.
evidence: This is supported by chloroquine resistance assays, fluorescence microscopy with cytosolic reporter, and electron microscopy data.

claim: In the absence of inflammasome responses, there is increased bacterial replication within vacuoles.
source: Notably, in the absence of inflammasome responses, we observed hyperreplication of Salmonella within the cytosol of infected cells as well as increased bacterial replication within vacuoles, suggesting that inflammasomes control Salmonella replication primarily within the cytosol and also within vacuoles.
evidence: This is supported by chloroquine resistance assays showing increased vacuolar bacteria in CASP1-/- cells.

claim: Inflammasomes control Salmonella replication primarily within the cytosol and also within vacuoles.
source: Notably, in the absence of inflammasome responses, we observed hyperreplication of Salmonella within the cytosol of infected cells as well as increased bacterial replication within vacuoles, suggesting that inflammasomes control Salmonella replication primarily within the cytosol and also within vacuoles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that loss of inflammasome components leads to increased bacteria in both compartments, with a greater increase in the cytosol.

claim: Salmonella is a major cause of food-borne illness worldwide.
source: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (Salmonella) is a facultative intracellular pathogen and a major cause of food-borne illness worldwide (Majowicz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Majowicz et al., 2010.

claim: Following ingestion, Salmonella colonizes the intestinal tract, where it can invade, replicate, and survive in host cells, including macrophages.
source: Following ingestion, Salmonella colonizes the intestinal tract, where it can invade, replicate, and survive in host cells, including macrophages (Crowley and Knodler, 2016; Santos and Bäumler, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Crowley and Knodler, 2016 and Santos and Bäumler, 2004.

claim: Salmonella employs type III secretion systems (T3SSs) that act as molecular syringes to inject virulence factors into the host cell cytosol.
source: Salmonella employs type III secretion systems (T3SSs) that act as molecular syringes to inject virulence factors, or effectors, into the host cell cytosol (Agbor and McCormick, 2011; Crowley and Knodler, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Agbor and McCormick, 2011 and Crowley and Knodler, 2016.

claim: Salmonella relies on two distinct T3SSs encoded on Salmonella Pathogenicity Islands 1 and 2 (SPI-1 and SPI-2) to invade and replicate within host cells, respectively.
source: Specifically, Salmonella relies on two distinct T3SSs encoded on Salmonella Pathogenicity Islands 1 and 2 (SPI-1 and SPI-2) to invade and replicate within host cells, respectively (Mills et al., 1995; Shea et al., 1996; Hensel et al., 1998; Galan and Zhou, 2000; Galán, 1999a; Galán and Collmer, 1999b; Galán and Curtiss, 1989; Ochman et al., 1996; Cirillo et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting the roles of SPI-1 and SPI-2.

claim: The SPI-2 T3SS translocates effectors to facilitate biogenesis and maintenance of the Salmonella-containing vacuole (SCV), wherein Salmonella resides and replicates.
source: The SPI-2 T3SS translocates effectors to facilitate biogenesis and maintenance of the Salmonella-containing vacuole (SCV), wherein Salmonella resides and replicates (Cirillo et al., 1998; Takeuchi, 1967a; Takeuchi and Sprinz, 1967b; Kihlström and Latkovic, 1978; Garcia del Portillo et al., 1993; Garcia del Portillo and Finlay, 1995; Steele Mortimer et al., 1999; Hansen Wester et al., 2002; Steele Mortimer, 2008; Jennings et al., 2017; Brumell et al., 2002a; Brumell et al., 2002b; Beuzón et al., 2000; Hensel et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting SCV biology.

claim: In epithelial cells, Salmonella escapes its vacuolar niche and hyperreplicates in the host cell cytosol.
source: In epithelial cells, Salmonella escapes its vacuolar niche and hyperreplicates in the host cell cytosol (Knodler et al., 2014a; Knodler et al., 2010; Knodler et al., 2014b; Malik Kale et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Knodler et al. and Malik Kale et al. studies.

claim: T3SS activity enables innate immune sensing of Salmonella.
source: While the activity of T3SSs are essential for Salmonella to infect and replicate within host cells, they also inject bacterial ligands that enable innate immune sensing of Salmonella (Miao et al., 2010b; Rayamajhi et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on inflammasome activation by T3SS components.

claim: The mammalian innate immune system detects violations of cytosolic sanctity through cytosolic pattern recognition receptors (PRRs).
source: The mammalian innate immune system detects violations of cytosolic sanctity, such as the presence of intracellular bacterial pathogens, through cytosolic pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) (Janeway, 1989; Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2009; Medzhitov and Janeway, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational immunology papers.

claim: NLR family proteins respond to their cognate stimuli by oligomerizing and inducing the assembly of multiprotein complexes termed inflammasomes.
source: NLRs respond to their cognate stimuli by oligomerizing and inducing the assembly of multiprotein complexes termed inflammasomes, which activate inflammatory caspases (Broz and Dixit, 2016; Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2009; Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2014; Martinon et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to inflammasome biology reviews and original research.

claim: Canonical inflammasomes recruit and activate caspase-1.
source: Canonical inflammasomes recruit and activate caspase-1, which cleaves and activates pro-inflammatory IL-1 family cytokines and the pore-forming protein gasdermin D (GSDMD) (Kuida et al., 1995; Li et al., 1995; Agard et al., 2010; Thornberry et al., 1992; Shi et al., 2015; Kayagaki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on caspase-1 function.

claim: Caspase-1 cleaves and activates pro-inflammatory IL-1 family cytokines and GSDMD.
source: Canonical inflammasomes recruit and activate caspase-1, which cleaves and activates pro-inflammatory IL-1 family cytokines and the pore-forming protein gasdermin D (GSDMD) (Kuida et al., 1995; Li et al., 1995; Agard et al., 2010; Thornberry et al., 1992; Shi et al., 2015; Kayagaki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on caspase-1 substrates.

claim: Noncanonical inflammasomes are formed by caspase-11 in mice and caspase-4 and caspase-5 in humans in response to cytosolic lipopolysaccharide (LPS).
source: Alternatively, noncanonical inflammasomes are formed by caspase-11 in mice and two orthologs in humans, caspase-4 and caspase-5, in response to cytosolic lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Casson et al., 2015; Hagar et al., 2013; Kayagaki et al., 2011; Kayagaki et al., 2013; Lagrange et al., 2018; Schmid Burgk et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on noncanonical inflammasome activation.

claim: Caspase-4, caspase-5, and caspase-11 directly process and activate GSDMD.
source: These caspases directly process and activate GSDMD (Kayagaki et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on GSDMD cleavage by inflammatory caspases.

claim: Liberated GSDMD N-terminal fragments oligomerize to create pores in the host plasma membrane.
source: Liberated GSDMD N-terminal fragments oligomerize to create pores in the host plasma membrane, through which IL-1 family cytokines and other alarmins are released to promote a lytic form of inflammatory cell death termed pyroptosis (Agard et al., 2010; Ding et al., 2016; Kayagaki et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on GSDMD pore formation.

claim: GSDMD pores allow release of IL-1 family cytokines and other alarmins to promote pyroptosis.
source: Liberated GSDMD N-terminal fragments oligomerize to create pores in the host plasma membrane, through which IL-1 family cytokines and other alarmins are released to promote a lytic form of inflammatory cell death termed pyroptosis (Agard et al., 2010; Ding et al., 2016; Kayagaki et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on pyroptosis mechanisms.

claim: Salmonella activates the NAIP/NLRC4 inflammasome in human macrophages.
source: Salmonella activates several inflammasomes in human macrophages. One such inflammasome is the NLR family, apoptosis inhibitory protein (NAIP)/NLR family, CARD domain-containing protein 4 (NLRC4) inflammasome (Bierschenk et al., 2019; Gram et al., 2021; Naseer et al., 2022a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on NAIP/NLRC4 activation by Salmonella.

claim: NAIP detects the cytosolic presence of T3SS structural components and flagellin.
source: NAIP detects the cytosolic presence of T3SS structural components and flagellin (Grandjean et al., 2017; Kofoed and Vance, 2011; Kortmann et al., 2015; Miao et al., 2010b; Molofsky et al., 2006; Rauch et al., 2016; Rayamajhi et al., 2013; Ren et al., 2006; Reyes Ruiz et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on NAIP ligand recognition.

claim: Upon ligand recognition, NAIP recruits NLRC4, which oligomerizes to form the active NAIP/NLRC4 inflammasome.
source: Upon ligand recognition, NAIP recruits NLRC4, which oligomerizes to form the active NAIP/NLRC4 inflammasome (Diebolder et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies of NAIP/NLRC4 inflammasome assembly.

claim: Salmonella activates the NLRP3 inflammasome in human macrophages.
source: Salmonella also activates the NLR pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome and the noncanonical caspase-4/5 inflammasome in human macrophages (Bierschenk et al., 2019; Casson et al., 2015; Gram et al., 2021; Naseer et al., 2022a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on NLRP3 activation by Salmonella.

claim: Salmonella activates the noncanonical caspase-4/5 inflammasome in human macrophages.
source: Salmonella also activates the NLR pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome and the noncanonical caspase-4/5 inflammasome in human macrophages (Bierschenk et al., 2019; Casson et al., 2015; Gram et al., 2021; Naseer et al., 2022a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on caspase-4/5 activation by Salmonella.

claim: NLRP3 responds to diverse stimuli, including ionic fluxes as a result of host plasma membrane damage.
source: NLRP3 responds to diverse stimuli, including ionic fluxes as a result of host plasma membrane damage (Franchi et al., 2007; Hornung et al., 2008; Mariathasan et al., 2006; Muñoz Planillo et al., 2013; Perregaux and Gabel, 1994), and can be secondarily activated by the noncanonical inflammasome (Baker et al., 2015; Casson et al., 2015; Kayagaki et al., 2013; Pilla et al., 2014; Rathinam et al., 2012; Rühl and Broz, 2015; Schmid Burgk et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on NLRP3 activation mechanisms.

claim: NLRP3 can be secondarily activated by the noncanonical inflammasome.
source: NLRP3 responds to diverse stimuli, including ionic fluxes as a result of host plasma membrane damage (Franchi et al., 2007; Hornung et al., 2008; Mariathasan et al., 2006; Muñoz Planillo et al., 2013; Perregaux and Gabel, 1994), and can be secondarily activated by the noncanonical inflammasome (Baker et al., 2015; Casson et al., 2015; Kayagaki et al., 2013; Pilla et al., 2014; Rathinam et al., 2012; Rühl and Broz, 2015; Schmid Burgk et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on crosstalk between noncanonical and NLRP3 inflammasomes.

claim: Inflammasome activation is critical for host defense against Salmonella.
source: Inflammasome activation is critical for host defense against Salmonella.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citations to in vivo and in vitro studies.

claim: In mice, the NAIP/NLRC4 inflammasome is required to control Salmonella infection.
source: In mice, the NAIP/NLRC4 inflammasome is required to control Salmonella infection (Carvalho et al., 2012; Franchi et al., 2012; Hausmann et al., 2020; Miao et al., 2006; Miao et al., 2010b; Rauch et al., 2016; Rauch et al., 2017; Sellin et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mouse infection studies.

claim: In murine intestinal epithelial cells (IECs), NAIP/NLRC4 inflammasome activation triggers pyroptosis and expulsion of infected cells.
source: In murine intestinal epithelial cells (IECs), NAIP/NLRC4 inflammasome activation triggers pyroptosis and expulsion of infected cells, and is both necessary and sufficient in IECs to restrict Salmonella replication and prevent bacterial dissemination to distal organ sites (Hausmann et al., 2020; Rauch et al., 2017; Sellin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on IEC responses to Salmonella.

claim: NAIP/NLRC4 inflammasome activation is both necessary and sufficient in murine IECs to restrict Salmonella replication and prevent bacterial dissemination to distal organ sites.
source: In murine intestinal epithelial cells (IECs), NAIP/NLRC4 inflammasome activation triggers pyroptosis and expulsion of infected cells, and is both necessary and sufficient in IECs to restrict Salmonella replication and prevent bacterial dissemination to distal organ sites (Hausmann et al., 2020; Rauch et al., 2017; Sellin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on IEC responses to Salmonella.

claim: Human epithelial cells do not rely on NAIP/NLRC4 or caspase-1, but instead rely on caspase-4 to control Salmonella replication.
source: Unlike murine IECs, human epithelial cells do not rely on NAIP/NLRC4 or caspase-1, but instead rely on caspase-4 to control Salmonella replication, in part through pyroptosis and cell extrusion (Holly et al., 2020; Knodler et al., 2014a; Knodler et al., 2010; Naseer et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on human epithelial cell responses to Salmonella.

claim: Human epithelial cells control Salmonella replication in part through pyroptosis and cell extrusion.
source: Unlike murine IECs, human epithelial cells do not rely on NAIP/NLRC4 or caspase-1, but instead rely on caspase-4 to control Salmonella replication, in part through pyroptosis and cell extrusion (Holly et al., 2020; Knodler et al., 2014a; Knodler et al., 2010; Naseer et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on human epithelial cell responses to Salmonella.

claim: In murine macrophages, inflammasome activation controls the replication of a mutant strain of Salmonella that aberrantly invades the cytosol.
source: Moreover, in murine macrophages, inflammasome activation controls the replication of a mutant strain of Salmonella that aberrantly invades the cytosol, but only slightly limits the replication of wild-type (WT) Salmonella (Man et al., 2014a; Thurston et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on murine macrophage responses to Salmonella.

claim: In murine macrophages, inflammasome activation only slightly limits the replication of wild-type (WT) Salmonella.
source: Moreover, in murine macrophages, inflammasome activation controls the replication of a mutant strain of Salmonella that aberrantly invades the cytosol, but only slightly limits the replication of wild-type (WT) Salmonella (Man et al., 2014a; Thurston et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on murine macrophage responses to Salmonella.

claim: Human macrophages rely on NAIP/NLRC4- and NLRP3-dependent inflammasome responses to control intracellular WT Salmonella replication.
source: In contrast, we found that human macrophages rely on NAIP/NLRC4- and NLRP3-dependent inflammasome responses to control intracellular WT Salmonella replication (Naseer et al., 2022a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Naseer et al., 2022a.

claim: WT THP-1 cells pretreated with YVAD had significantly reduced levels of IL-1β release compared to infected WT cells pretreated with the vehicle control.
source: Upon infection with wild-type (WT) Salmonella, WT THP-1 cells pretreated with either YVAD or ZVAD had significantly reduced levels of IL-1β release and cell death compared to infected WT cells pretreated with the vehicle control (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: WT THP-1 cells pretreated with ZVAD had significantly reduced levels of IL-1β release compared to infected WT cells pretreated with the vehicle control.
source: Upon infection with wild-type (WT) Salmonella, WT THP-1 cells pretreated with either YVAD or ZVAD had significantly reduced levels of IL-1β release and cell death compared to infected WT cells pretreated with the vehicle control (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: WT THP-1 cells pretreated with YVAD had significantly reduced cell death compared to infected WT cells pretreated with the vehicle control.
source: Upon infection with wild-type (WT) Salmonella, WT THP-1 cells pretreated with either YVAD or ZVAD had significantly reduced levels of IL-1β release and cell death compared to infected WT cells pretreated with the vehicle control (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by LDH release assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: WT THP-1 cells pretreated with ZVAD had significantly reduced cell death compared to infected WT cells pretreated with the vehicle control.
source: Upon infection with wild-type (WT) Salmonella, WT THP-1 cells pretreated with either YVAD or ZVAD had significantly reduced levels of IL-1β release and cell death compared to infected WT cells pretreated with the vehicle control (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by LDH release assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pretreatment with YVAD largely phenocopies ZVAD in THP-1 cells infected with Salmonella.
source: Since pretreatment with YVAD largely phenocopies ZVAD, these data suggest that caspase-1 is the primary caspase that responds to Salmonella infection in THP-1 cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar effects of YVAD and ZVAD on IL-1β release and cell death.

claim: Caspase-1 is the primary caspase that responds to Salmonella infection in THP-1 cells.
source: Since pretreatment with YVAD largely phenocopies ZVAD, these data suggest that caspase-1 is the primary caspase that responds to Salmonella infection in THP-1 cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar effects of YVAD (caspase-1 inhibitor) and ZVAD (pan-caspase inhibitor).

claim: The increase in bacterial CFUs was significantly higher in WT cells pretreated with YVAD compared to cells pretreated with DMSO.
source: The increase in bacterial CFUs was significantly higher in WT cells pretreated either YVAD or ZVAD compared to cells pretreated with DMSO (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The increase in bacterial CFUs was significantly higher in WT cells pretreated with ZVAD compared to cells pretreated with DMSO.
source: The increase in bacterial CFUs was significantly higher in WT cells pretreated either YVAD or ZVAD compared to cells pretreated with DMSO (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: WT cells treated with YVAD prior to infection harbored significantly higher intracellular Salmonella burdens compared to cells pretreated with DMSO.
source: Microscopic analysis revealed that WT cells treated with either YVAD or ZVAD prior to infection harbored significantly higher intracellular Salmonella burdens compared to cells pretreated with DMSO (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: WT cells treated with ZVAD prior to infection harbored significantly higher intracellular Salmonella burdens compared to cells pretreated with DMSO.
source: Microscopic analysis revealed that WT cells treated with either YVAD or ZVAD prior to infection harbored significantly higher intracellular Salmonella burdens compared to cells pretreated with DMSO (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Caspase-1 activity primarily controls Salmonella burdens in human macrophages.
source: Overall, these results suggest that caspase-1 activity primarily controls Salmonella burdens in human macrophages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of caspase-1 inhibition on bacterial burdens.

claim: WT THP-1 cells primed with Pam3CSK4 and then infected with WT Salmonella exhibited high levels of IL-1β release at 6 hpi.
source: In agreement with previous reports (Bierschenk et al., 2019; Gram et al., 2021; Naseer et al., 2022a), WT THP-1 cells primed with Pam3CSK4 and then infected with WT Salmonella exhibited high levels of IL-1β, IL-18, and IL-1α release as well as cell death at 6 hpi (Figure 1A–B; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: WT THP-1 cells primed with Pam3CSK4 and then infected with WT Salmonella exhibited high levels of IL-18 release at 6 hpi.
source: In agreement with previous reports (Bierschenk et al., 2019; Gram et al., 2021; Naseer et al., 2022a), WT THP-1 cells primed with Pam3CSK4 and then infected with WT Salmonella exhibited high levels of IL-1β, IL-18, and IL-1α release as well as cell death at 6 hpi (Figure 1A–B; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: WT THP-1 cells primed with Pam3CSK4 and then infected with WT Salmonella exhibited high levels of IL-1α release at 6 hpi.
source: In agreement with previous reports (Bierschenk et al., 2019; Gram et al., 2021; Naseer et al., 2022a), WT THP-1 cells primed with Pam3CSK4 and then infected with WT Salmonella exhibited high levels of IL-1β, IL-18, and IL-1α release as well as cell death at 6 hpi (Figure 1A–B; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: WT THP-1 cells primed with Pam3CSK4 and then infected with WT Salmonella exhibited cell death at 6 hpi.
source: In agreement with previous reports (Bierschenk et al., 2019; Gram et al., 2021; Naseer et al., 2022a), WT THP-1 cells primed with Pam3CSK4 and then infected with WT Salmonella exhibited high levels of IL-1β, IL-18, and IL-1α release as well as cell death at 6 hpi (Figure 1A–B; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by LDH release assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pam3CSK4-primed CASP1-/- THP-1 cells released negligible levels of inflammasome-dependent cytokines upon infection.
source: In contrast, Pam3CSK4-primed CASP1-/- THP-1 cells released negligible levels of inflammasome-dependent cytokines and did not undergo substantial cell death upon infection (Figure 1A–B; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: Pam3CSK4-primed CASP1-/- THP-1 cells did not undergo substantial cell death upon infection.
source: In contrast, Pam3CSK4-primed CASP1-/- THP-1 cells released negligible levels of inflammasome-dependent cytokines and did not undergo substantial cell death upon infection (Figure 1A–B; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by LDH release assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Infected WT and CASP1-/- THP-1 cells released similar levels of the inflammasome-independent cytokine TNF-α.
source: Infected WT and CASP1-/- THP-1 cells released similar levels of the inflammasome-independent cytokine TNF-α (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Caspase-1 is required for inflammasome responses to Salmonella infection in human macrophages.
source: These results indicate that caspase-1 is required for inflammasome responses to Salmonella infection in human macrophages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the loss of IL-1 cytokine release and cell death in CASP1-/- cells.

claim: At 1 hpi, there were no significant differences in bacterial uptake between Pam3CSK4-primed WT and CASP1-/- THP-1 cells.
source: At 1 hr post-infection (hpi), we did not observe any significant differences in bacterial uptake between Pam3CSK4-primed WT and CASP1-/- THP-1 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: At 6 hpi, CASP1-/- cells harbored significantly higher bacterial burdens compared to WT cells.
source: However, at 6 hpi, CASP1-/- cells harbored significantly higher bacterial burdens and a significant fold-increase in bacterial CFUs compared to WT cells (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: At 6 hpi, CASP1-/- cells showed a significant fold-increase in bacterial CFUs compared to WT cells.
source: However, at 6 hpi, CASP1-/- cells harbored significantly higher bacterial burdens and a significant fold-increase in bacterial CFUs compared to WT cells (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: WT cells contained relatively low numbers of Salmonella on average (~5 bacteria per cell) at 6 hpi.
source: WT cells contained relatively low numbers of Salmonella on average (~5 bacteria per cell), while CASP1-/- cells harbored significantly higher numbers of Salmonella on average (~30 bacteria per cell) at 6 hpi (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: CASP1-/- cells harbored significantly higher numbers of Salmonella on average (~30 bacteria per cell) at 6 hpi.
source: WT cells contained relatively low numbers of Salmonella on average (~5 bacteria per cell), while CASP1-/- cells harbored significantly higher numbers of Salmonella on average (~30 bacteria per cell) at 6 hpi (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Caspase-1 limits intracellular Salmonella replication in human macrophages.
source: Overall, these data indicate that caspase-1 limits intracellular Salmonella replication in human macrophages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased bacterial burdens in CASP1-/- cells.

claim: At 1 hpi, there were no significant differences in bacterial uptake between unprimed WT and CASP1-/- THP-1 cells.
source: At 1 hpi, we did not observe any significant differences in bacterial uptake between unprimed WT and CASP1-/- THP-1 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: At 6 hpi, unprimed CASP1-/- cells harbored significantly higher bacterial burdens compared to unprimed WT cells.
source: However, at 6 hpi, unprimed CASP1-/- cells harbored significantly higher bacterial burdens and a significant fold-increase in bacterial CFUs compared to unprimed WT cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-C.

claim: At 6 hpi, unprimed CASP1-/- cells showed a significant fold-increase in bacterial CFUs compared to unprimed WT cells.
